lessons.title: Common Fish Diseases and Parasites
lessons.body: In Africa, the most common fish diseases in tilapia and catfish farms are bacterial infections like Aeromonas and Streptococcus, which cause ulcers, fin rot, and sudden death. Fungal infections like Saprolegnia appear as cotton-like tufts on skin or eggs, often after handling or poor water quality. Parasites include Ichthyophthirius (white spot), Trichodina, and gill flukes. White spot looks like tiny grains of salt on skin and gills; fish scratch against walls and gasp at the surface. Gill flukes cause pale gills, excess mucus, and gasping. You can check for parasites by placing a gill clipping or skin scrape on a microscope slide with a drop of water. A cheap 40x-100x microscope costs about $50-100 and is essential. For bacteria, look for red spots, open sores, swollen belly, or bulging eyes (exophthalmia). Streptococcus often causes erratic swimming, curved spine, and eye cloudiness. In catfish, Aeromonas hydrophila is common after stress from handling or poor water quality. Fungal infections follow injury. To confirm, use a simple dipstick for ammonia and nitrite; high levels stress fish and trigger disease. Prevention is cheaper than treatment: keep ammonia below 0.5 mg/L, nitrite below 0.3 mg/L, and pH 6.5-8.5 for tilapia. Stock at 3-5 fish per square meter for tilapia in ponds, or 100-150 fish per cubic meter in tanks with aeration. Overstocking is the number one cause of disease outbreaks. Observe fish daily during feeding; sick fish stop eating. Remove dead fish immediately. If you see white spot, raise water temperature to 30Â°C for 5-7 days (if species tolerate it) and add salt at 3-5 g/L. For bacterial ulcers, improve water quality first; then use oxytetracycline at 50 mg/kg fish per day for 7-10 days in feed. Always check local regulations on antibiotic use. In Africa, many farmers use potassium permanganate at 2-4 mg/L as a bath for external parasites, but it stains and can kill fish if overdosed. Always test on a few fish first.

lessons.title: Biosecurity Measures in Fish Farms
lessons.body: Biosecurity means keeping diseases out of your farm and stopping them from spreading. In Africa, where wild fish and farmed fish often share water, this is critical. Start with your water source. If you use river or lake water, filter it through a 200-500 micron mesh screen to keep out wild fish and eggs. Better yet, use borehole or well water. If you must use surface water, treat it with chlorine at 10-20 mg/L for 24 hours before use, then dechlorinate with sodium thiosulfate at 1 mg/L per 1 mg/L chlorine. But chlorine kills everything, including beneficial bacteria, so only use it for empty ponds or tanks. For incoming fish, always quarantine new stock for 14-21 days in a separate tank. Never mix new fish with existing stock directly. Keep different age groups separate: fry, fingerlings, and adults each in their own ponds or tanks. This prevents disease transfer from older carriers to young fish. Limit visitors. Provide boots and hand sanitizer at the entrance. A footbath with 2% sodium hypochlorite (bleach) solution at the gate works. Change it daily. Keep birds, frogs, and snakes out with netting or fencing. These animals carry parasites and bacteria. Clean and disinfect nets, buckets, and aerators between ponds. Use a 200 mg/L bleach solution for 30 minutes, then rinse and sun-dry. Sun-drying is free and kills many pathogens. For ponds, drain and dry for 1-2 weeks between cycles. If you cannot drain, apply agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) at 100-200 kg per hectare to raise pH and kill pathogens. In Africa, many farmers share equipment; this spreads disease. Own your own nets and boots if possible. If not, disinfect before and after each use. Record all fish movements, deaths, and treatments in a notebook. This helps you spot patterns. Vaccination is part of biosecurity, but only for specific diseases like Streptococcus in tilapia. Good biosecurity reduces antibiotic use, which saves money and keeps fish safe for consumers. Remember, one sick fish can kill your whole crop. Act fast: isolate, test, and treat.

lessons.title: Diagnosing Fish Health Issues
lessons.body: Diagnosing fish health problems starts with daily observation. Spend 10 minutes at each pond or tank, especially at feeding time. Healthy fish swim actively and eat well. Sick fish may gasp at the surface, swim erratically, scrape against walls, or hide. Look for physical signs: red spots, ulcers, fin rot, white spots, cotton-like growths, swollen belly, bulging eyes, or pale gills. Check water quality first. Use a test kit for ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH, and temperature. Ammonia above 0.5 mg/L and nitrite above 0.3 mg/L are toxic. Low oxygen (below 3 mg/L for tilapia) causes gasping. High nitrates (above 100 mg/L) stress fish. If water quality is poor, fix that before treating disease. Next, examine a few sick fish. Catch them gently with a soft net. On a clean surface, look at gills: lift the gill cover. Healthy gills are bright red; pale or brown gills mean anemia or parasites. Use a microscope to check for parasites. A skin scrape: hold fish with wet hands, gently scrape mucus from side with a clean slide, add a drop of water, cover slip, and view at 40x-100x. You will see moving protozoa like Trichodina or Ichthyophthirius. For gills, cut a small piece and do the same. For bacteria, you need a lab to culture, but you can guess from symptoms. Streptococcus causes eye cloudiness, curved spine, and erratic swimming. Aeromonas causes red ulcers and fin rot. Fungal infections look like cotton wool. If you suspect a virus, like Tilapia Lake Virus (TiLV), you will see lethargy, skin lesions, and high mortality. There is no treatment for viruses; cull and disinfect. In Africa, many farmers lack labs. Work with your local fisheries officer or university. They can test samples for a small fee. Take photos and record deaths. A simple necropsy: open the belly, check liver, spleen, and kidney for spots or swelling. Keep a notebook with dates, water parameters, symptoms, and actions. This helps you learn and prevent future outbreaks. Early diagnosis saves fish and money.

lessons.title: Treatment Methods: Chemicals and Antibiotics
lessons.body: When fish get sick, treat fast and correctly. First, improve water quality: increase aeration, reduce feeding by half, and do a 30% water change. Many diseases clear up when water quality is good. For external parasites like white spot and Trichodina, use salt (sodium chloride) at 3-5 g/L as a bath for 5-7 days. For a 1000-liter tank, that's 3-5 kg of salt. Dissolve it first, then add. Salt is cheap and safe if dosed correctly. For gill flukes, use formalin at 25 ml per 1000 liters as a bath for 1 hour with strong aeration, then flush. Formalin is toxic; wear gloves and ventilate. Potassium permanganate at 2-4 mg/L as a bath for 30 minutes treats external parasites and fungi. It turns water purple; if it turns brown quickly, organic load is high, so re-dose carefully. For fungal infections, salt or formalin works. For bacterial infections, antibiotics are sometimes needed. Oxytetracycline is common: mix at 50 mg per kg of fish per day for 7-10 days. For a 100 kg fish biomass, use 5 g of oxytetracycline in feed daily. Mix with a little oil to bind, then coat feed. Do not use antibiotics preventively; this causes resistance. Only use when you see clear bacterial signs like ulcers or fin rot, and confirm with a vet if possible. Florfenicol at 10 mg/kg fish per day for 10 days is another option. Always follow withdrawal periods: oxytetracycline needs 21 days before harvest for human consumption. In Africa, many drugs are unregulated; buy from reputable suppliers and check expiry dates. Never use chloramphenicol or malachite green; they are banned for food fish. For internal parasites, use praziquantel at 2-5 mg/kg fish in feed for 3 days. For external wounds, apply iodine or salt directly on ulcers. Always test treatments on a few fish first. Keep records of treatment, date, dose, and results. If fish do not improve in 3 days, re-evaluate. Overdosing kills fish; underdosing fails and breeds resistance.

lessons.title: Vaccination and Immunization
lessons.body: Vaccination protects fish from specific diseases before they get sick. In Africa, the most available vaccine is for Streptococcus agalactiae in tilapia. This bacterium causes massive mortalities, up to 50% in some farms. The vaccine is given by injection or immersion. For injection, you need to anesthetize fish first with clove oil at 40-50 mg/L. Then inject 0.1 ml of vaccine into the intraperitoneal cavity (belly) using a 23-25 gauge needle. This is labor-intensive but gives strong immunity. For small fish, immersion vaccination is easier: dip fish in a diluted vaccine solution for 30-60 seconds. This works for fry and fingerlings. The vaccine must be stored at 2-8Â°C and used before expiry. In Africa, vaccines can be expensive and hard to find. Check with your fisheries department or veterinary office. Some countries have local production. If you cannot get vaccines, focus on biosecurity and good management. Vaccination is not a substitute for clean water and low stress. Also, vaccines only work if fish are healthy. Do not vaccinate sick fish. Vaccinate at the right age: for tilapia, vaccinate fingerlings at 10-15 g. Booster doses may be needed for long grow-out. For catfish, vaccines are less common, but research is ongoing. In Kenya, Egypt, and Nigeria, some commercial farms use autogenous vaccines (made from killed bacteria from their own farm). This requires a lab. If you make your own, follow strict safety. Remember, vaccines cause stress. Handle fish gently, use anesthesia, and keep them in clean water after. Monitor for 24 hours. Some fish may die from handling, but the long-term protection is worth it. Keep records: vaccine type, batch number, date, and fish size. If you see disease despite vaccination, it might be a different strain. Work with a vet to diagnose. Vaccination reduces antibiotic use, which is good for your wallet and for consumers. Start small: vaccinate a few tanks and compare with unvaccinated. If it works, expand.

lessons.title: Quarantine and Isolation Protocols
lessons.body: Quarantine means keeping new or sick fish separate to prevent disease spread. Every fish farm in Africa should have a quarantine tank or pond. When you buy new fish, never put them directly into your main pond. Set up a separate tank, at least 100 liters for small batches, with its own net, bucket, and aerator. Keep it away from other ponds, ideally under shade. Quarantine for 14-21 days. During this time, observe daily for symptoms: white spots, ulcers, abnormal swimming, or lack of appetite. Test water quality every 2 days. If fish look healthy after 21 days, you can move them. But first, do a preventive dip: salt bath at 5 g/L for 5 minutes, or potassium permanganate at 2 mg/L for 30 minutes. This kills external parasites. For sick fish in your main pond, isolate them immediately. Use a separate tank or a hapa (net enclosure) within the pond but away from healthy fish. Better yet, remove them to a hospital tank. Treat according to diagnosis. Do not return them until they are disease-free for at least 7 days. If you have a disease outbreak, stop all water flow between ponds. Use separate nets and boots for each pond. Disinfect equipment with bleach (200 mg/L) after use. If many fish die, cull and bury or burn carcasses far from water. Do not throw dead fish into rivers or ponds. In Africa, where sharing water is common, quarantine is your best defense. For tilapia, a quarantine tank can be a 1m x 1m x 1m concrete tank or a 1000-liter plastic tank with a small filter. Keep water temperature stable at 26-28Â°C. Feed lightly. Record everything: date in, source, number, symptoms, treatments, date out. If you cannot afford a separate tank, use a hapa in a corner of a pond, but ensure no water exchange. Quarantine also applies to plants and equipment. New plants can carry parasites; dip them in salt water (10 g/L for 2 minutes) before adding. Always assume new fish carry something. It is better to lose a few fish in quarantine than your whole stock.

quiz.q: What is the most common bacterial disease in African tilapia farms?
quiz.explanation: Streptococcus causes major mortalities in tilapia, while the others are fungal, parasitic, or viral.

quiz.q: Which parasite appears as tiny white spots on fish skin and gills?
quiz.explanation: Ichthyophthirius, or white spot, is characterized by salt-like grains on skin and gills.

quiz.q: What is the recommended salt dose for treating white spot in a 1000-liter tank?
quiz.explanation: A salt bath of 3-5 g/L for 5-7 days is effective and safe for most fish.

quiz.q: Which water quality parameter should be kept below 0.5 mg/L to prevent stress?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia above 0.5 mg/L is toxic and predisposes fish to disease.

quiz.q: What is the number one cause of disease outbreaks in fish farms?
quiz.explanation: Overstocking leads to poor water quality and stress, triggering disease.

quiz.q: Which chemical is used as a bath for external parasites but stains water purple?
quiz.explanation: Potassium permanganate at 2-4 mg/L treats parasites and turns water purple.

quiz.q: How long should new fish be quarantined before adding to main stock?
quiz.explanation: A 14-21 day quarantine allows symptoms to appear and prevents disease introduction.

quiz.q: Which antibiotic is commonly used for bacterial infections in fish?
quiz.explanation: Oxytetracycline is approved for fish, while chloramphenicol and malachite green are banned.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for oxytetracycline before harvest?
quiz.explanation: A 21-day withdrawal ensures no antibiotic residues remain in fish for human consumption.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is available for tilapia in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Streptococcus agalactiae vaccine is commercially available for tilapia in some African countries.

quiz.q: How is the Streptococcus vaccine usually administered to fingerlings?
quiz.explanation: Immersion for small fish and intraperitoneal injection for larger fish are common methods.

quiz.q: What should you do first when you see sick fish in a pond?
quiz.explanation: Poor water quality is often the root cause; fix it before treating disease.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for diagnosing parasites on fish?
quiz.explanation: A microscope at 40x-100x allows you to see protozoa and flukes on skin or gills.

quiz.q: What does a cotton-like growth on fish skin indicate?
quiz.explanation: Saprolegnia and other fungi appear as cotton-like tufts, often after injury.

quiz.q: Which biosecurity measure prevents disease entry from visitors?
quiz.explanation: A footbath with 2% sodium hypochlorite at the entrance disinfects boots and limits pathogen spread.

quiz.q: How long should ponds be dried between cycles to kill pathogens?
quiz.explanation: Sun-drying for 1-2 weeks is a free and effective way to reduce pathogens in pond bottoms.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dose of agricultural lime for pond disinfection?
quiz.explanation: Applying 100-200 kg/ha of calcium carbonate raises pH and kills many pathogens.

quiz.q: Which parasite causes pale gills and excess mucus?
quiz.explanation: Gill flukes attach to gills, causing anemia, excess mucus, and gasping.

quiz.q: What is the correct treatment for internal parasites?
quiz.explanation: Praziquantel at 2-5 mg/kg fish in feed for 3 days treats internal parasites.

quiz.q: Why should you never use chloramphenicol in food fish?
options: B) It is banned and harmful to humans
quiz.explanation: Chloramphenicol is banned due to risk of aplastic anemia in humans.

quiz.q: What is an autogenous vaccine?
options: A) A vaccine made from local pathogens
B) A vaccine from another country
quiz.explanation: Autogenous vaccines are made from killed bacteria isolated from the farm's own fish.

quiz.q: How long should you observe fish after vaccination?
quiz.explanation: Monitor for 24 hours post-vaccination to check for adverse reactions or handling stress.

quiz.q: What is a hapa?
options: A) A type of net enclosure
quiz.explanation: A hapa is a net enclosure used for quarantine or holding fish within a pond.

quiz.q: Which disinfectant is used for equipment in biosecurity?
quiz.explanation: A 200 mg/L bleach solution disinfects nets, buckets, and boots effectively.

quiz.q: What is the first step when diagnosing fish disease?
options: B) Observe behavior and check water
quiz.explanation: Daily observation and water testing are the foundation of diagnosis.

quiz.q: Which virus causes high mortality in tilapia with no treatment?
quiz.explanation: Tilapia Lake Virus (TiLV) has no treatment; culling and disinfection are necessary.

quiz.q: What is the recommended salt concentration for a preventive dip?
quiz.explanation: A 5 g/L salt dip for 5 minutes kills external parasites on new fish.

quiz.q: Why is vaccination not a substitute for biosecurity?
options: B) Vaccines only work for some diseases
quiz.explanation: Vaccines target specific pathogens, but good water quality and hygiene prevent many other diseases.

quiz.q: What should you do with dead fish during an outbreak?
options: B) Bury or burn far from water
quiz.explanation: Burying or burning carcasses prevents spreading pathogens to other fish or water sources.

quiz.q: Which water parameter should be tested every 2 days during quarantine?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia and nitrite are toxic; testing every 2 days ensures water quality in quarantine tanks.
